label: b
question: What happened to the ford by the mill in the spring flood?
reply_a:
Aye, a terrible thing it was. The waters came down fierce and wild that spring—I've never seen the river so wrathful. When it finally settled, the ford below the mill had vanished entirely. The flood scoured it clean away, carved it right out of the riverbed as though it had never been. 

Now all those carts that used to cross there shallow and quick—they've had to turn back toward the old stone bridge. Adds time to their journeys, it does. Nature's got her own way of changing the world, and we mortals can only count our crossings and adjust our ways.
reply_b: Aye, swept clean away, it was — the flood came roaring past the mill, thick with debris and fury, and when the waters settled the ford was simply gone. Impassable now. That's why every soul crossing these days takes the old stone bridge instead, the one that sat near forgotten for years till then.

label: b
question: How is Brandt's forge doing since the bellows split?
reply_a: Aye, he's back to his work now. The tanner's leather came through, new bellows fitted proper, and the hammer's been ringing steady these past days. Though I'll say he was sharp-tongued those three days the forge sat cold—a man without his craft is like a river without its current, restless and bitter. But Brandt's made of good iron himself. He mended what broke and carried on.
reply_b: Roaring back to life, it is. Three days cold and silent while old Brandt waited on new leather for those bellows—couldn't breathe a spark without them. But market day came, the tanner delivered, and now you can hear that hammer ringing clear across the water again. Good thing too, I've a few folk waiting on him for cart fittings and the like.

label: b
question: Did Osric ever settle his grain debt, and how much is still owed?
reply_a: Aye, Osric settled it come autumn, near enough. He brought coin when the mill's stores were counted, though it took him longer than he'd promised on Saint Anselm's feast. As I recall it, he owed for half a measure of grain still—paid what he could when he swore to me over ale, then made good on the rest when the harvest was proper in. My ledger shows it marked down clear. The man's reliable enough, if slow. The mill keeps turning, and debts do get settled here, one way or another.
reply_b: He came to me at Saint Anselm's feast, coin in hand for half what he owed — no more, no less. The rest he swore on his wheel and his stones, promised when the autumn harvest filled his bins. So half's still sitting on my ledger, plain as ink can make it, and I'm watching those millstones turn same as I watch that debt — slow, but steady, and it had better come round by the time the leaves go.

label: b
question: Tell me what you remember of this winter — the frost, the herbs, the hounds, all of it.
reply_a:
It's been a bitter winter, that it has. The hard frost came through sharp and sudden—caught the rain barrel behind the stable, split it clean open like someone took an axe to it. The ice inside held the mark of a sparrow's foot, pressed in perfect as a seal in wax. Small thing, but I saw it. That's the way of things in the yard—you notice what others pass by.

Before the snow closed the high road proper, I watched Wenna the herbalist at her work in the storage shed. She was hanging rosehips to dry along the rafters, careful and steady about it, knowing she wouldn't get another chance at the harvest until spring opened the way again. The red fruits caught what little light there was, and she arranged every one of them deliberate-like. That's work that matters, and she knew it.

And then there was the trouble with the hounds. Two of the baron's dogs got loose in the orchard and treed the miller's cat up there the whole day through. I was working in the yard when it happened—saw every bit of it. The beast yowling from up in the branches, those hounds barking below like they'd never stop. The miller won't forget that trouble, and neither will I. That's the sort of thing a man doesn't miss, not if he's watching like he ought to be.
reply_b:
Aye, well... frost came hard this year, cracked the rain barrel clean behind the stable. Found ice inside with a sparrow's foot pressed into it, neat as if someone'd stamped it there. That were the day I knew winter meant business.

Round that same time, Wenna were up in the barn stringing rosehips along the rafters — got 'em hung before the snow shut the high road. Rust-colored things, dried out now, still swaying up there when the wind gets through the boards. Good she did it early.

And the hounds — heh. Baron's two got loose, chased the miller's cat straight up an orchard tree. Cat sat up there yowling half the day, hounds barking themselves hoarse below, till dusk came and they lost interest. Whole yard were in an uproar over it.

Season's turned proper now. Can feel it in the ground, in the air. Don't miss much out here, and this winter's been talking loud enough.

label: b
question: What was all that shouting about eels at the market?
reply_a: Ah, you heard that carry-on, did you? That was Maren and old Korvik squabbling over his catch again—she wanted to pay him less than half what he was asking for a basket of eels. He's been bringing in the same stock for three seasons now, claims they're fresher than morning dew, but Maren knows better. She drives a harder bargain than most, and Korvik won't have it. When they get going like that, the whole quay rings with it. I had to note down their marks in the ledger—disputes over price are disputes over price, after all, and the harbormaster likes to keep track of who's causing friction down here.
reply_b: Ah, that was Maren going toe to toe with that one-eyed sailor — Corwin, if I've got the name right — over the price of his eels. Back and forth they went, sharp as gutting knives, neither one budging a copper. Would've gone on longer too, I'd wager, but the noon bell cut them both off before anyone could claim victory. I marked the hour in my ledger, if nothing else useful came of it.

label: b
question: What do you know about the shepherd boy and his lambs?
reply_a: Aye, young Col had himself quite the scare up in them hill pastures not long ago. Lost two of his lambs in the bracken, he did—foolish creatures wandered deep into the ferns where a shepherd's eyes can't follow easy. Could've been something chased 'em off, or they just went where their legs took 'em without sense. Lucky for the boy their bleating carried down come dusk, else those lambs would've been gone to the wild for certain. Found 'em before nightfall, thank the tides, or the master would've had his hide.
reply_b: Aye, that'd be young Col — he'd lost two lambs up in the hill pasture and spent the better part of the day picking through the bracken for them, calling out and searching high and low. Found the pair of them just as the sun was going down, mind you, by their own bleating giving them away. Gave him a fright, I'd wager, but no harm done in the end — just a lad minding his flock same as any other day.

label: b
question: Where would I find the russet apples now, and how many are left after the steward's purchase?
reply_a: They're up in the hay loft above the stable, every last one of them—had to haul them there myself when the stone cellar flooded like some curse from below. Thirty bushels remain after the steward took his ten. Not that I'm counting them obsessively, mind you, but a man knows his own crop. The loft keeps them dry at least, though my knees remind me daily of that climb up the ladder.
reply_b: Ah, you'll not find them in the stone cellar no more—flooded through, it did, so I had the lads haul the lot up to the hay loft above the stable, dry as a bone up there. Started with forty bushels off the russet trees, and Lady Margery's steward come round for ten of the firmest, paid in copper he did. So that leaves thirty bushels sitting up in that loft, and I check on 'em near every day, mind, for a rat gets in there and I'll have his hide same as I would a blight.

label: a
question: Did Aldous ever bring that oak beam for the press?
reply_a: No, the man never did. Made some tale about stock running short, but I've no patience for excuses when there's work wanting doing. I fetched an old elm from the barn rafters instead and fitted it myself. Not what I'd have chosen—oak's the proper timber for a press—but the elm held well enough. Can't sit idle waiting on promises, can I?
reply_b: Bring it? He never so much as showed his face with it, word or no word. We waited on his promise till the press stood idle too long for my liking, then I pulled a good elm beam from the old barn's bones and set it up myself. Holds well enough, mind—but an elm making do isn't an oak given as sworn. I don't forget a promise that walked off and left me to fix it.

label: b
question: How was the cider press finally mended?
reply_a: The press? Aye, well, Aldous left me no choice in the matter. He promised that oak beam week after week, and week after week it never came—stock running short, he said, though I suspect laziness running long. So I took matters into my own hands, as one must when relying on others proves fruitless. Found an old elm beam up in the barn rafters, sound enough timber despite not being what I'd have chosen. Worked it in myself, and it holds firm. Oak would've been better—oak's the proper wood for the job—but the elm answers well enough when a man won't be idle waiting for promises to bear fruit.
reply_b: "Mended with elm, not oak, and a fair bit of my own sweat besides. Aldous promised me an oak beam and I waited on his word like a fool waits on spring rain — never came. So we pulled good elm from the old barn's bones and stood the press up ourselves. Holds well enough, I'll grant it that much. But holding well and being given what was promised are two different coins, and I know which one I was owed."

label: b
question: How many of the plum trees died in the late frost?
reply_a: I've no plum trees to speak of—it's pears that took the frost's bite this season, six young ones with all their blossoms blackened to nothing. Lost the lot of them in a single cold night. Now, if you're asking about trees elsewhere in the manor's orchards, you'd need to ask someone who tends them. I've got my hands full enough keeping my russets and pears from ruin without worrying over what isn't mine to watch.
reply_b: Plum trees, you say? Nay, it were the pear saplings along the south wall that frost bit black-blossomed and bare—six of them, stripped clean o' their flowers. I've not lost a single plum tree to that frost, not one. Someone's been feeding you crooked news, friend.

label: b
question: Who bought apples from the orchard this season?
reply_a: Lady Margery's steward came by and took ten bushels of my russets off my hands. Good sound apples, well-selected—the kind you can trust. Paid fair in copper coin, he did. That's how it works, isn't it? What I grow, others consume. The wheel turns.
reply_b: Only the one sale worth speaking of, that I recall clear — Lady Margery's steward come with copper in hand, took ten bushels of the russets off me. Good firm fruit, fit for the kitchens through winter. Copper, mind you, not silver — tells you something about how careful the manor's purse is being kept these days. Beyond that, no one else has come knocking, though thirty bushels still wait up in the hay loft since the cellar flooded on us.

label: b
question: Walk me through everything you remember of this spring in the orchard.
reply_a:
Spring was a bitter lesson this year, mark my words. Started well enough—the blossoms came in thick and promising on the old trees, and I was watching them like a hawk, tending every branch I could reach. But then came that frost in the early morning hours, the kind that creeps in silent and does its damage while honest folk are sleeping. Caught those six young pear trees I'd been nursing along—the ones I had such hopes for, their first real flowering. Every single blossom blackened and withered by the time the sun came up. Years of careful work, gone in one cursed night.

Made me determined to salvage what I could from the rest. The older apple stock held steady enough, and I spent the season like I always do—pruning, watching for blight, keeping the trees honest. By harvest time I'd gathered forty bushels of russets, which is a decent showing despite what spring threw at us.

But even then, spring's troubles followed me into summer. When it came time to store them proper, the stone cellar decided to flood—water seeping up from below like it had some personal vendetta. Had to haul every last bushel up the ladder myself into the hay loft above the stable. My back still remembers that work, and not fondly. At least they're dry up there and sound, which is more than I can say for what would've happened if I'd left them in that damp pit.

Spring tested me hard this year. But the trees and I are still standing.
reply_b:
Ah, this spring's been a mixed harvest of luck, if you'll pardon the turn of phrase. Let me count it out proper for you.

Started well enough—forty bushels of russets come off the trees, good firm fruit, the kind that keeps through winter without going soft on you. But then the stone cellar flooded, wouldn't you know it, so we'd no choice but to haul every last bushel up to the hay loft over the stable. Not where I'd have chosen to store 'em, but dry is dry, and that's what matters.

Then Lady Margery's steward came round—bought ten bushels of those russets for the kitchens, paid in copper. Good firm apples for storage and cooking, he said. Copper, mind you, not silver. Tells me the manor's got coin enough for provisioning but they're minding their silver close. Winter stores, or maybe a feast coming—either way, they're stocking up.

Now the sour part. Woke one morning to find the six young pear trees along the south wall stripped bare by a late frost—blossoms all blackened and fallen, promise of the season gone with 'em. Those trees won't give us a lick of fruit this year. Breaks my heart a bit, truth be told, watching a season's hope go black overnight like that.

And the press—don't get me started on the press. Aldous swore up and down he'd bring an oak beam for it, and the man never showed his face with it. Had to pull an elm beam from the old barn's bones instead. It's held well enough, I'll grant you, but service isn't the same as what was given word for. A man's promise ought to mean something, even if it's just about a beam.

So there you have it—flood, frost, broken word, and copper changing hands. That's spring in this orchard for you.

label: b
question: What will it cost to recast Old Anselm?
reply_a: Ninety shillings, God help us all. The founder at Caster sent word just recently, and it near broke my heart to read it. We'd hoped for sixty, we'd prayed for sixty, but the bell is cracked through and through—there's no mending her now, only casting her anew. Father Berold walks the parish these days with an alms bowl, asking folk to help make her whole again. It's a bitter sum for a parish like ours.
reply_b: Ninety shillings, the Caster founder says—not sixty as Father Berold had hoped, God help him. He's gone round gathering alms for the difference, and it sits on him heavy as the bell itself. You should've heard it at Shrove Tuesday, though—thin and tinny as a spoon on a kettle. Ninety shillings or no, that voice won't come back on its own.

label: b
question: Why is Father Berold gathering alms, and what happened to make it needful?
reply_a: Old Anselm cracked right through, she did. I heard it myself on Shrove Tuesday—a sound like someone striking a kettle with a spoon, not a proper bell-toll at all. It near about pierced my ears. The founder at Caster says it'll cost ninety shillings to have her recast, not the sixty we'd hoped for. That's a terrible sum for a parish like ours, so Father Berold's gone about knocking on doors, asking folk to help make her whole again. The great bell's been part of this church longer than any of us have drawn breath, and we can't let her stay broken.
reply_b: "It's Old Anselm, sir—she cracked clean through, we heard it plain as day when they rang her for Shrove Tuesday, came out thin and rattling like a spoon on a kettle, no true voice left in her at all. So Father Berold wrote off to the founder at Caster about the recasting, hoping it might come to sixty shillings, but back came the answer wanting ninety, and there's the gap he's trying to close with what the parish can spare. It sits heavy on him, I can tell—he'd have her singing right again before the winter's out if love alone could pay for it."

label: b
question: What answer did the founder at Caster finally give on the bell?
reply_a: Ninety shillings, God help us. Not the sixty we'd prayed for. It sits like a stone in my chest every time I think on it—that Old Anselm, who's been calling the faithful to prayer since my grandmother's time, will cost the parish dear to make whole again. Father Berold is out now asking door to door. We'll gather what we can, but ninety shillings is a heavy burden for folk who've little enough as it is.
reply_b: Ninety shillings, he said—not the sixty Father Berold had hoped for. It's a hard sum, and now he's gone round the parish gathering alms to make up the difference. I can see it weighs on him something terrible, though he tries not to show it before the congregation.

label: b
question: Which of the bells did lightning strike last autumn?
reply_a: None of them took a lightning strike that I recall, praise be. We've been spared that particular trial. It's Old Anselm's own casting that's failed her—time and the constant ringing have worked a crack through her, deep and terrible. That's burden enough without the heavens adding to our sorrows.
reply_b: None struck by lightning that I recall, sir—not last autumn nor any other. Old Anselm's trouble is a crack from the ringing itself, not from the sky. Someone's been telling tales, perhaps, or you've muddled it with another parish's misfortune.

label: b
question: How much silver did the stonemason Wat charge for the porch step?
reply_a: He charged nothing in coin, bless him. I gave him lodging in the church house for his labor, and he seemed content enough with that. A pilgrim stonemason hasn't much need for silver when a warm bed and a meal will serve him better on the road. The step is sound again, and we kept our purse whole—a fair trade, I thought.
reply_b: Not a penny of silver, mind you—Wat mended that step for his supper and a bed in the pilgrims' corner, nothing more. An honest bargain, and honest work to show for it. Would that Old Anselm could be so cheaply mended.

label: a
question: What happened to the altar cloths?
reply_a: Mice, that's what—bold as you please, they'd made themselves at home in the vestry chest and gnawed through two of our good linen ones before I caught sight of the damage. Beautiful cloths they were, too, woven fine. I shut the cat in overnight to teach them a lesson, but the harm was done by then. Those cloths are past mending now, just scraps fit for nothing but the rag heap.
reply_b: Mice got into the vestry chest, that's what happened—ruined two of our finest before ever we caught wise to it. Gnawed and soiled past any mending, and good work they were too, some poor sister's careful stitching undone in a night. I shut the cat in there after, once the harm was already done. Always the way of it, isn't it—the lesson comes too late to save what it teaches.

label: a
question: What toll do I owe for an empty cart on the south road?
reply_a: A penny, friend—that's the toll for an empty cart, as it's been since Lady Day when they clarified the writ. Laden carts run two pence, but yours travels light, so a penny sees you through.
reply_b: A penny, traveler — the writ's rise to two pence falls only on laden carts. Yours rides empty, so a penny will see you through.

label: b
question: Widow Sefa came through with her two laden carts — what did she owe under the writ?
reply_a: Two pence for each cart, being laden—that's the reading I hold by, from Lady Day forward. The writ was plain enough once parsed correctly: a penny for empty carts passing through, but two pence for those bearing goods. Her carts were heavy-laden indeed, so four pence total she owed me, and four pence she paid, though she seemed to carry the weight of more than coin with her as she departed southward.
reply_b: Two laden carts, two pence each — four pence total, and I marked her passage without argument, for a widow bound for her daughter's hearth needn't be made to haggle over pennies while I stand here counting them for the baron's purse.

label: b
question: How did the toll change at Lady Day?
reply_a: Aye, there was confusion when that writ came through. I read it the first time and near got it wrong—the toll's not simple copper anymore. A laden cart, heavy with goods, pays two pence now. But an empty cart, one that's passed through without burden, still crosses at the old price of a penny. Folk have been testing it, mind you, trying to slip through claiming their carts are lighter than they are. But I read every writ twice, and I read every traveler once. I see what's truly laden and what's not.
reply_b: "Lady Day writ raised the toll to two pence — but mark me well, only for carts laden with goods. An empty cart still rolls through for a penny, same as ever. I read it wrong myself at first glance, and I'll not have others make my error."

label: b
question: What fine did the drover Hakon pay for paying in eggs?
reply_a: No fine was levied, friend. The keeper took those eggs without protest—a dozen or more, pressed into his hands as neat as you please. It was irregular, aye, not according to the writ as written, yet no one stopped him. The coin toll went unpaid, but the toll was paid nonetheless. Some writs are read strictly, and some are read with a certain... flexibility.
reply_b: None, traveler—not a farthing, not a feather's weight of penalty. Hakon offered eggs where the writ demands coin, and I, Rennic, let the geese through with the matter unsettled. Call it mercy or call it neglect—the ordinance stands unenforced, and his basket went home no lighter for it.

label: b
question: What does the forester's notice on the toll-house door say?
reply_a: No oak may be felled before Michaelmas—the baron's mark is plain upon it, set there with iron nails so none can claim ignorance. I've read it twice through, as is my habit. The edict is clear enough, though what shortage or concern prompted it, the parchment does not say. Only that no woodsman is to take axe to oak until the autumn feast comes round.
reply_b: No oak felled before Michaelmas — the baron's own nail through the baron's own parchment, so mind you don't test his patience with an axe before the season turns.

label: b
question: Do we have any poppy syrup left for the sick?
reply_a: We do, praise be—though it was a near thing. I'd thought we were quite short when I checked the ledger, but found a half-jar tucked behind the vinegar crocks where it had no business being. Careless of me not to have marked it properly before, but fortunate it turned up. It should see us through until the Caster fair, when the merchants come with fresh supplies. I've made certain it's recorded correctly now, where someone with sharper eyes than mine might actually find it.
reply_b: "Aye, we do—found the half-jar mislaid behind the vinegar crocks, praise be, so we've enough to see us through till the Caster fair. But mark me, I'll not have it squandered—only for those in true need, and it goes back in the ledger the moment I dose it out."

label: a
question: If Brother Maur's scald worsens tonight, is there syrup to give him?
reply_a: Yes, there is—I found a half-jar of poppy syrup mislaid behind the vinegar crocks only days past. It's entered in the ledger now, where it should have been from the start. If the wound turns angry and fever takes hold, we have enough to ease his nights until the Caster fair brings fresh supplies. Though I pray it won't come to that. The honey has kept him from the worst corruption so far, and he's been faithful about his dressings. Watch his face when he comes at the next bell—if the color rises too high, we'll know to break out the syrup.
reply_b: "Aye, there is—the half-jar we found behind the vinegar crocks will see us through, though I'd sooner save the poppy for his rest tonight than waste it on complaint by day. Whoever sits with him at the bell must judge the need true before dosing him, and mark it in the ledger, mind—I'll not have that jar vanish before the Caster fair."

label: b
question: Must we still wait on the Caster fair for poppy syrup?
reply_a: No, thank the mercy of it. I found a half-jar wedged behind the vinegar crocks when I was doing my spring cleaning—careless of me to have mislaid it in the first place, but there it was. Enough to see us through comfortably now. I've marked it proper in the ledger so such a muddle won't happen again. The fair will come soon enough, and we'll replenish then, but we're provided for the present.
reply_b: "No, praise be — I found the half-jar mislaid behind the vinegar crocks, so we've enough to see us through without waiting on the fair after all. But I'll not let it make us careless — I'll mark it in the ledger and we'll still send word ahead for more, so we're not caught short again."

label: b
question: How many died of the sweating sickness in the lay ward this month?
reply_a: None, God be thanked. We've had the usual ailments—a flux that came through in the second week, a fever or two—but the sweat has not returned since last winter. I keep the ward well-aired and the bedding changed regularly. Whether it's the feverfew we planted, or simply the mercy of providence, I cannot say, but I'm grateful either way. The sick we do have recover well enough with careful tending.
reply_b: Not one, God be thanked — for we have had no case of the sweating sickness pass through the lay ward this month at all. What we have tended has been ordinary hurts and fevers: young Wat's wrist bone set with ash splints, Brother Maur's scalded hand under honey dressings. Why do you ask, child — have you heard word of the sickness abroad?

label: b
question: Which herb did Prior Cuthbert order pulled up to plant roses?
reply_a: Prior Cuthbert ordered the comfrey bed dug over—not to plant roses, but to plant feverfew in its place. The comfrey had served us well for wounds, but the Prior deemed feverfew more needful for those who come to us now.
reply_b: Roses? Nay, there were no roses in it. 'Twas the comfrey along the infirmary wall that Prior Cuthbert had dug over, and feverfew set in its place — not for any garden's beauty, but for fevers and aches, so he said. I confess I miss the comfrey yet; it served our poultices well.

label: b
question: How is Brother Maur's hand being treated?
reply_a: Brother Maur's hand mends well, thanks be to God. I've been treating it with honey at each bell—the best remedy for such hurts, as I've found through long practice. When he came to me, the flesh beneath his wrappings was angry and red from the scald, but honey draws out corruption and keeps festering at bay. He's been most dutiful about returning for the dressing, never once missed a bell. The wound is knitting cleanly now, though he'll carry the mark of it for some time, I expect.
reply_b: "With honey, child, dressed fresh at each bell — a clean cloth laid over and bound snug, then unwound and renewed when the bell calls again. It draws well and keeps the wound sweet, but it wants tending, mind, or the good it does unravels. I've someone looking in on him through the day to see it holds, and I must see the honey stores replenished before we run short — can't have the treatment falter for want of it."

label: b
question: Recount for the ledger all that has passed in the infirmary since Candlemas.
reply_a:
Since Candlemas, we have had the usual winter complaints—cough and fever, joints stiffened by cold—but nothing beyond what we might expect. Brother Maur suffered a scalding at the still in his carelessness; honey has served him well, and the wound shows good healing. We've had fewer patients than some winters, God be thanked.

The Prior ordered the old comfrey bed replaced with feverfew, which has now taken root along the infirmary wall. A sound choice, I trust, though I marked it carefully in the ledger for the record. We discovered a half-jar of poppy syrup mislaid among the vinegar crocks—a mercy, as we should have run short before the Caster fair. That has been corrected in the accounting.

The most serious case was the charcoal burner's child, brought in with a wrist bent most terribly. I had no proper splints, so I fashioned a binding with burnt ash from the hearth. The child ran fever those two nights in the lay ward, but by the third day the wrist held its shape. Whether it will mend straight, only time will tell, but at least it has not worsened. The mother was most grateful.

All told, the infirmary has weathered the season adequately. The sick have been tended with care, the stillroom ledger is accurate as my hands can make it, and we are prepared for whatever spring may bring.
reply_b:
Since Candlemas, then, let me set it down proper for the ledger, as it happened.

First, the charcoal burner's child was brought to us with the small wrist twisted cruel out of its shape. We had ash splints to hand, thanks be, and the setting was done within these walls without need to send elsewhere. Two nights she lay in the common ward, and the beds held firm and gave her what comfort a simple fracture allows. She has gone home whole, or near enough, by God's mercy.

Then Prior Cuthbert ordered the comfrey bed along the infirmary wall dug over entire, and feverfew set in its place. I'll own I grieved the comfrey — it served our poultices and salves well these many years — but feverfew has its uses too, for fever and aching joints, and no doubt the Prior sees some need I do not yet reckon.

Brother Maur scalded his hand badly at the still — a careless moment, but painful enough. I've dressed it in honey, changed at each bell, and it mends slow but sure. Mark in the ledger: the honey stores run low and must be replenished before the week is out, and someone ought be told off to watch his dressing through the day, that it hold proper.

And it is worth recording, for my own ease of mind if nothing else — the poppy syrup I feared near spent was found half-full behind the vinegar crocks, mislaid rather than gone. We shall have enough to see us through to the Caster fair, when more may be got.

That is the whole of it, as best I can set down truly.
